meta.title: Who really said "The only question with wealth is, what do you do with it?"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Credited to John D. Rockefeller Sr., but Wikiquote traces it to his son, John D. Rockefeller Jr., in Fosdick's 1956 portrait — and the wording is reworded.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The only question with wealth is, what do you do with it?'?
meta.ogDescription: Wrong Rockefeller: the line is his son John D. Rockefeller Jr.'s, documented in Fosdick's 1956 portrait and printed in TIME that September.

answer.label: Not John D. Rockefeller Sr. — actually his son, John D. Rockefeller Jr.
answer.authorDates: 1874–1960 · American philanthropist, only son of John D. Rockefeller Sr.
answer.sourceLine: Wikiquote files this line in the Misattributed section of its John D. Rockefeller page and identifies it as a statement of his son, John D. Rockefeller Jr., as quoted in Raymond B. Fosdick’s John D. Rockefeller, Jr., a Portrait (Harper, 1956), p. 189. The documented sentence reads “The only question with wealth is what to do with it” — and TIME’s profile of Rockefeller Jr. on 24 September 1956 ↗ prints it as “what you do with it.” The circulating interrogative form, “what do you do with it?”, matches neither exactly.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: John D. Rockefeller, Jr., a Portrait
Raymond B. Fosdick · Harper, New York, 1956 · p. 189 (page as cited by Wikiquote)

source.excerpt: I was born into it [wealth] and there was nothing I could do about it. It was there, like air or food or any other element. The only question with wealth is what to do with it. It can be used for evil purposes or it can be an instrumentality for constructive social living.
trail: Wikiquote’s John D. Rockefeller page ↗ puts this exact sentence in its Misattributed section: credited to the Sr. in a 2006 investing book by Chris M. Hart, but “clearly a statement of his son,” quoted in Fosdick’s John D. Rockefeller, Jr., a Portrait (1956), p. 189.
Wikiquote’s John D. Rockefeller Jr. page ↗ carries the same line as a sourced Jr. quote from the 1956 Fosdick biography, inside the fuller “I was born into it” passage.

TIME’s 24 September 1956 profile of Rockefeller Jr. ↗ prints the same passage in the “what you do with it” form. It is not a second, independent witness: the profile was written around Fosdick’s newly published Harper biography, which it credits in a footnote.
The cited book is real and datable: the Internet Archive scan ↗ and the Rockefeller University catalogue record ↗ both give Raymond B. Fosdick, Harper, New York, 1956.
source.excerptNote: This is the wording Wikiquote quotes from Fosdick’s 1956 portrait, including the closing line about wealth serving either evil purposes or constructive social living. TIME’s profile of 24 September 1956 ↗ carries the same passage with the key clause changed — “what you do with it” for “what to do with it” — and stops before that closing line. Neither source states the occasion, audience or year of the remark itself; TIME says only that “he once explained.”

author.heading: About John D. Rockefeller Jr.
author.metaLine: 1874–1960 · American philanthropist · only son of John D. Rockefeller Sr.
author.bio: John Davison Rockefeller Jr. (born 29 January 1874, died 11 May 1960) was the only son of Standard Oil co-founder John D. Rockefeller Sr., and he spent his life on the giving side of the family fortune rather than the earning side. Wikipedia records donations of more than $537 million across his lifetime, including the reconstruction of Colonial Williamsburg, the development of Rockefeller Center, and land purchases donated to national parks such as Grand Teton, Acadia and Great Smoky Mountains. That biography — inherited money, deliberately redirected — is exactly what makes this sentence his rather than his father’s.

misattribution.heading: What’s wrong with the popular version
misattribution.intro: Two things are off at once: the wrong man is credited, and the sentence has been re-punctuated into a question.

items.why: Wikiquote lists the line in the Misattributed section of its John D. Rockefeller page ↗, noting it appears credited to the Sr. in a 2006 stock-market book by Chris M. Hart, and stating that it is clearly a statement of his son, John D. Rockefeller Jr., as quoted in Fosdick’s 1956 portrait, p. 189.
Neither documented text asks a question. Fosdick’s biography has “what to do with it” (per Wikiquote’s sourced entry ↗), and TIME’s 24 September 1956 profile ↗ has “what you do with it.”

AZQuotes files the interrogative version under John D. Rockefeller Sr. (1839–1937) ↗ and gives its source as IMDb’s personal-quotes page — not a Rockefeller document. The same page separately lists the longer “I was born into it” passage, also under the father.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is a Rockefeller’s — just the son’s, not the father’s: John D. Rockefeller Jr., on the fortune he inherited ↗.

context.heading: Why this one gets pinned on the wrong Rockefeller
lead: There are two John D. Rockefellers, and the quote market keeps collapsing them into one. The father (1839–1937) founded Standard Oil and assembled the fortune; the son (1874–1960) inherited it and spent a lifetime deciding what to do with it. A line about the obligation of money reads like a founder’s epigram, but it is really an heir’s problem statement — and that is precisely how Rockefeller Jr. framed it.

In the fuller passage he is almost apologetic about the fortune: it was simply there, he says, “like air or food or any other element.” The sentence people now quote is the pivot in that thought, not a boast about being rich. Stripped of the surrounding lines and re-pointed as a rhetorical question, it loses the thing that made it interesting.
context.detailsSummary: The three wordings, side by side
detailsBody: Fosdick, 1956 (the cited biography): “The only question with wealth is what to do with it.”
TIME, 24 September 1956: “The only question with wealth is what you do with it.”
What circulates online: “The only question with wealth is, what do you do with it?” — credited to the father, and punctuated as a question he never asked.
context.pull: An heir’s problem statement, not a founder’s epigram.
